questions.passage: On the morning of the district science fair, Maya Chen arrived at the gymnasium before the doors opened. She carried a tri-fold board titled “Shade and Surface: Measuring Heat in Our Schoolyard” and a shoebox of thermometers wrapped in foam. Her project had begun three weeks earlier, when she noticed that the blacktop outside the cafeteria was too hot to touch while the grass beneath the oak trees felt cool. Her first plan—to place eight thermometers around campus—collapsed when the custodian, Mr. Alvarez, explained that the school’s insurance rules forbade students from working alone outdoors. Maya felt the familiar tightness in her chest. Then Mr. Alvarez offered to supervise during lunch. They measured at noon on three days, recording temperatures on asphalt, concrete, grass, and wood chips. The asphalt was consistently hottest, but Maya was surprised that wood chips stayed nearly as warm as concrete. At the fair, a judge in a green jacket asked why she had not tested sand. Maya’s face went hot. She admitted that she had expected wood chips to behave like shade. The judge nodded, not unkindly, and asked what she would change. Maya pointed to a corner of her board where she had written, “Next time: test materials under the same amount of sun, and include sand.” The judge’s pencil moved across his clipboard. When he moved to the next table, Maya did not relax. She rechecked her data, and for the first time noticed that the grass readings varied by more than the asphalt readings. She wrote a note in her notebook. By the time the gym emptied, her board had a small white tag: “Honorable Mention, Earth and Space Science.” Maya tucked it into her pocket. What pleased her most was not the tag but the note she had made: a question she had not known she would want to answer.
questions.q: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Maya learns that she should have tested sand instead of using thermometers.
Maya decides that science fair judges favor projects about asphalt and concrete.
Maya comes to value revising her work and asking new questions more than the recognition she receives.
Maya discovers that the school’s safety rules make original research impossible.
questions.explanation: Maya’s attention at the end is on the note she wrote, not the award, and her experience shows her growing willingness to revise her methods and pursue a new question. The passage does not claim that the rules make research impossible or that sand was the project’s focus; those details serve her scientific development.

questions.passage: Before my junior year, I believed that history was a list of dates and that good students memorized the list quickly. I signed up for Mr. Haruki Tanaka’s U.S. History class because the counselor said it counted for graduation, not because I expected to enjoy it. On the first day, Mr. Tanaka wrote four words on the board: Who gets to decide? Then he passed out two accounts of the same 1911 factory fire, one from a newspaper owned by the factory owner and one from a workers’ newsletter. I raised my hand to ask which account was correct. He said, “That is the assignment.” For the next month, I was annoyed. I wanted answers; he gave us footnotes. But something shifted when we studied a local rent strike. Mr. Tanaka brought in a folder of city council minutes from the 1970s. The minutes were dry, but the margins contained handwritten notes from residents—names, complaints, and a grocery list on one page. He asked us to reconstruct what the minutes left out. I stayed after class for three days, not because my grade needed it but because I could not stop thinking about a woman named Mrs. Elena Cortez, whose name appeared in the margin five times and in the official transcript not at all. By senior year, I had joined the speech team. My first tournament topic was school funding, and I found myself doing what Mr. Tanaka had trained us to do: reading outside the official report, comparing claims, asking who benefited. I did not win the tournament. I did win something less visible: a habit of suspicion toward easy summaries. Now, when friends say they hate history because it is just memorization, I explain that bad history may be a list, but good history is an argument about power. Mr. Tanaka did not give me that sentence. He made me work for it.
questions.q: Which statement best expresses the main theme of the passage?
options: Competition is more valuable than classroom instruction in developing students’ thinking.
Historical accounts are usually identical once they are carefully read.
Students learn history best when they avoid official documents altogether.
Education can transform a student’s habits of mind by making the student notice whose voices are absent from official records.
questions.explanation: The narrator’s growth comes from learning to compare accounts and investigate omissions, such as Mrs. Cortez’s missing name. The passage does not urge students to avoid official documents entirely or claim that historical accounts are usually identical.

questions.passage:
Tucson's summer monsoon turns dry washes into ribbons of green, but for desert wildlife those ribbons are also a maze of curbs, driveways, and traffic. A proposal before the city council would fund a network of small wildlife corridors—strips of native plants and carefully placed underpasses—to connect patches of open space. Some residents worry that the plan spends too much money on animals. Yet the corridor proposal is less a luxury than a practical investment in public safety.
Consider the Arroyo Seco pilot project. After the city installed two underpasses beneath a busy road and planted native mesquite and brittlebush along a half-mile stretch, a volunteer survey recorded 38 percent fewer vehicle collisions involving deer over three years. The same survey found that javelinas and coyotes were using the underpasses regularly. These changes did not eliminate traffic, but they reduced the dangerous moments when animals and drivers meet at high speed.
Corridors also help species adapt as heat and drought reshape the desert. When habitat is broken into isolated patches, small populations lose access to food and mates. Native plantings can provide shade and seeds while linking those patches. A corridor need not be large. A narrow chain of protected yards and median plantings can function as a stepping-stone route.
The council should approve the modest $420,000 pilot expansion. For comparison, the city spends more than that each year repairing vehicles damaged by wildlife collisions. Supporting wildlife and protecting drivers are not competing goals; they are two results of the same careful design.
questions.q: The author's attitude toward the corridor proposal can best be described as:
options: nostalgic, wishing that Tucson had remained undeveloped
impartial, presenting costs and benefits without recommending a course of action
supportive, emphasizing its practical benefits
doubtful, suggesting that the plan is too expensive to justify
questions.explanation: The author calls the corridor proposal "less a luxury than a practical investment in public safety" and concludes that the council should approve the pilot expansion, so the voice is supportive and practical. The passage does not remain neutral or favor abandoning the plan; it repeatedly connects conservation with driver safety.

questions.passage:
On the morning we moved, our apartment in Cleveland looked smaller than it ever had. The boxes stacked by the door seemed to swallow the living room, and the pale rectangle where our couch had stood glowed like a footprint. Mama taped the last box shut and wrote KITCHEN on the side in her neat, square letters. My little brother, Mateo, sat on the empty floor, tracing the swirls in the carpet as if he could memorize them.
The new house was forty minutes east, in a town whose name I had practiced saying until it sounded ordinary. It had a maple tree in the front yard and a bedroom for each of us, which Mama called the whole point. Baba carried the first box inside and stopped in the hallway, listening. The house was so quiet that I could hear the refrigerator hum and Mateo breathing through his mouth. At the apartment, Mrs. Alvarez's television had always murmured through the wall, and someone was always laughing in the stairwell.
While Mama and Baba argued gently about where the table should go, I walked upstairs. My room had a window facing the maple. A previous family had left a row of pencil marks on the doorframe, each labeled with a name and a date. I touched the highest mark and imagined a kid stretching on tiptoe to add it. Then I found a pencil in my backpack and made a small mark near the bottom—just my name and the year.
Downstairs, the phone rang. It was Abuela, who had promised to visit once the boxes were gone. Mama put her on speaker, and we all stood in the kitchen, hearing Abuela complain about the distance and then admit she was already packing a bag. Mateo began to cry, not because he was sad, but because the sound of her voice made the strange house feel for a moment like it had always been ours.
questions.q: The passage is narrated from the point of view of:
options: the narrator's younger brother, Mateo
a neighbor who watches the family unpack from outside
a member of the family who is moving into the new house
Abuela, who is packing a bag to visit the family
questions.explanation: The narrator uses I and describes her own actions and observations while the family moves into the new house, including walking upstairs and marking the doorframe. The narrator is not Mateo, Abuela, or a neighbor watching from outside.

questions.passage:
When Nia Calderón bought the old Bellamy Building for her print shop, the contractor warned her about the plaster. It was from 1911, he joked, and it had opinions. On the third morning, a hammer broke through the wall near the stairwell, and a bundle wrapped in oilcloth slid to the floor. Inside were sixty-seven postcards, a brass stencil, and a notebook with a list of names written in three inks.

Nia had planned to spend the afternoon choosing ink colors. Instead, she sat on a paint bucket and read. The notebook belonged to a stationer named Hattie M. Tso, who had rented the ground floor from 1912 to 1929. Tso's entries recorded orders for wedding invitations, church programs, and signs for a union meeting. On one page, she had written: 'M. Okafor paid 50 cents. Do not let her carry the parcel; her brother will.' Another page listed a dozen names under the heading 'small jobs, no charge.' Nia recognized two names from the town's war memorial and one from a street sign.

The contractor wanted to know whether to keep breaking plaster. Nia asked him to stop. She carried the bundle downstairs and placed it on the counter, feeling oddly formal, as if Hattie Tso might walk in and ask for it back. By evening, Nia had found a photograph in the town archive: a narrow storefront with a hand-lettered window reading 'Tso Printing & Notions.' The figure in the doorway was blurred, but the sign was unmistakable.

The building had always seemed to Nia like a shell that other people had used and left. Now the walls seemed less empty than crowded. She did not know whether the postcards were unsold stock or thank-you notes never sent. But she knew the notebook was not trash. She called the historical society, then she went back to work. Before she inked her first poster that week, she set the brass stencil on the shelf above her press, where she could see it.
questions.q: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
options: A contractor's carelessness leads to the destruction of valuable documents.
A business owner regrets buying an old building after discovering its history.
An unexpected find in a building gives its new owner a deeper sense of connection to the past.
A historical society must persuade a printer to donate a collection of artifacts.
questions.explanation: The passage centers on Nia's discovery of Hattie Tso's notebook and the change in how Nia sees the building. It concludes with Nia keeping the stencil where she can see it, showing that the past now feels present to her. The passage does not say she regrets the purchase or that the contractor destroys the documents.

questions.passage:
When workers repairing the foundation of the Fayette County courthouse in eastern Texas uncovered a layer of gray limestone, they expected a routine job. Instead, a paleontologist named Dr. Lena Ortiz noticed small, circular patterns on a broken slab. They looked like the cross sections of coral. That seemed unlikely: the courthouse sits roughly 100 miles from the Gulf of Mexico, and the limestone had been quarried locally in the 1890s.

Ortiz sent samples to a lab, which dated the rock to about 115 million years ago, when a shallow sea covered much of what is now central Texas. The coral-like shapes turned out not to be coral at all but rudist bivalves, thick-shelled mollusks that built reefs in ancient oceans. Unlike modern reefs, which are dominated by coral, rudist reefs were built by these clams, some of which grew as tall as 30 centimeters. Their shells accumulated in mounds that eventually became the limestone used in the courthouse.

The discovery did not change the courthouse's age, but it changed how Ortiz thought about the quarry. The masons who cut the stone in the 1890s likely saw the fossil patterns as flaws. Some slabs were probably rejected; others were used where their markings would be hidden. Ortiz and her students later found similar fossils in three nearby barns and a church step, suggesting that local quarries supplied far more fossil-bearing stone than records showed.

Ortiz's conclusion was simple: a building can be a natural history museum if no one has labeled the exhibits. The courthouse still serves its original purpose, but its foundation now tells two stories at once—the story of a town and the story of an ocean that disappeared long before the town existed.
questions.q: According to the passage, rudist bivalves differed from the organisms that build most modern reefs in that rudist bivalves were:
options: limited to shallow water rather than deep ocean.
smaller than most modern reef builders.
clams rather than coral.
found only in Texas rather than around the world.
questions.explanation: The passage explains that the coral-like shapes were not coral but rudist bivalves, which are thick-shelled mollusks, and that modern reefs are dominated by coral. It does not compare the groups by depth, overall size, or geographic range.

At dawn on the first Saturday of October, Mateo’s grandmother, Abuela Luz, set a chipped blue bowl on the kitchen table and announced that the calabaza were ready. The field behind the barn had gone gold overnight, or so it seemed, to Mateo, who had spent the summer complaining that the vines were taking over the fence. Now he walked between rows with a pair of pruning shears, cutting each squash at an angle the way Abuela had taught him: not straight across, she insisted, because a slanted cut kept water from pooling in the stem. His cousin Ivy joined them after breakfast, her sneakers already muddy. She carried a red wagon and a radio, and she sang loudly enough that the dog barked.

By noon the wagon held twenty-three squash, six bundles of herbs, and a bucket of late tomatoes. Mateo’s arms ached, but he did not want to stop. The air smelled of dry corn silk and diesel from the tractor, and beyond the fence Mr. Delgado’s crew was picking soybeans in long, noisy sweeps. At the end of the row, Abuela held up a small, crooked squash and called it the best one. Mateo laughed. It was the sort of squash that would never appear in a grocery store, too bent to stack neatly, but Abuela set it aside for the pot.

That evening, the kitchen filled with steam. Abuela roasted the crooked squash with garlic and lime, and Ivy stirred a pot of black beans while Mateo warmed tortillas on the comal. When Mr. Delgado knocked at the back door with a jar of honey, he stayed for dinner. They ate outside at a picnic table, the radio playing between songs and commercials. No one mentioned the work still waiting in the field. questions.q: As used in the passage, the word pooling most nearly means:
options: swimming
spreading
draining
collecting
questions.explanation: The passage explains that a slanted cut kept water from pooling in the stem; in this context, pooling means collecting or gathering in one place. The nearby mention of water and a cut stem supports that meaning rather than swimming, spreading, or draining.

questions.q: The passage most strongly suggests that Mateo’s view of the harvest has changed by the end of the passage because he
options: decides that the crooked squash should not be used for dinner
wants to leave the field to avoid Mr. Delgado’s crew
believes the vines have stopped growing over the fence
finds satisfaction in the food and company that the harvest makes possible, not just in completing chores

questions.q: The passage is narrated from which point of view?

Third-person omniscient, revealing the thoughts of every character

questions.passage:
When the cafeteria at Rosa Parks Middle School closed its kitchen at 2 p.m., the ovens sat idle until morning. Last fall, our family and consumer science teacher, Ms. Alvarez, proposed using them for a weekly supper club: students, families, and nearby volunteers would cook a simple meal together and eat it in the cafeteria. Some administrators worried about cost and liability. The first semester, however, answered those concerns more clearly than any speech could.

The club ran for twelve Thursdays. A local grocery donated vegetables that were still fresh but too ripe for weekday display; the school’s maintenance staff found the ovens needed only a routine cleaning, not repairs; and the PTA covered $3 per person for ingredients, far less than the $9 average cost of a fast-food meal. More than forty families participated, and the cafeteria’s waste dropped because students learned to use stems, peels, and leftovers in stock and sauces. Seventh grader Nia Chen said she had never liked collard greens until she helped wash and tear them herself. Her father, who works two jobs, told the club’s coordinator that Thursday was the only evening he did not eat alone.

The club did not solve every problem. It required careful scheduling, and volunteers had to complete a short food-safety training. Yet the benefits were not abstract. Students practiced measuring, budgeting, and teamwork; families met neighbors they otherwise passed only in the pickup line; and the kitchen became a place of shared purpose rather than a locked room. If the school board wants a low-cost way to strengthen community and teach practical skills, it should make the supper club a permanent program. The empty ovens are not neutral; they are a resource waiting to be used.
questions.q: Which of the following best states the main claim of the passage?
options: The school cafeteria should close early so that the ovens can be cleaned routinely.
Fast-food meals are too expensive for most families at Rosa Parks Middle School.
Students should avoid eating collard greens unless they help prepare them.
The school should make the supper club permanent because it provides low-cost community and educational benefits.
questions.explanation: The final paragraph explicitly urges the school board to make the supper club permanent because it is a low-cost way to strengthen community and teach practical skills. The other statements either reverse the passage’s position or focus on minor details.
